easy.text: Why is water considered a 'polar' molecule?

options.text: It has an uneven distribution of electric charge across the molecule
options.feedback: Correct -- the oxygen end is slightly negative and the hydrogen ends are slightly positive.

options.text: It is always found at the North and South Poles
options.feedback: This confuses geographic poles with the chemistry meaning of 'polar.'

options.text: It has no charge at all anywhere on the molecule
options.feedback: Polar molecules actually have regions of charge -- a truly chargeless molecule would be nonpolar.
Polarity is a property of the water molecule itself, regardless of what state (solid, liquid, gas) it's in.

medium.text: Because of its polarity, water molecules are attracted to each other through what type of force?

options.feedback: Correct -- the slightly positive hydrogen of one water molecule attracts the slightly negative oxygen of another.
While gravity exists everywhere, the special attraction between water molecules is due to hydrogen bonding, not gravity.
Water molecules aren't magnetic -- their attraction comes from charge differences, not magnetism.
Nuclear forces act within an atom's nucleus, unrelated to how separate water molecules attract each other.

hard.text: Why does water have an unusually high boiling point compared to other similarly small molecules?

options.text: Hydrogen bonds between water molecules require extra energy to break before boiling can occur
options.feedback: Correct -- the strong hydrogen bonding network in water demands more energy input to separate molecules into vapor.

options.text: Water molecules are unusually heavy compared to other small molecules
options.feedback: Water is actually a fairly light molecule -- its high boiling point is due to bonding forces, not mass.

options.text: Water contains a rare, exotic element
options.feedback: Water is made of common hydrogen and oxygen -- its high boiling point comes from intermolecular attraction, not exotic elements.

options.text: Water molecules repel each other, requiring extra energy to separate
options.feedback: Water molecules actually attract each other strongly (via hydrogen bonds); it's this attraction, not repulsion, that raises the boiling point.

easy.hard: One part of the molecule carries a slightly different charge than the rest.
easy.medium: One end of the molecule is slightly negatively charged, and the other end is slightly positive.
easy.easy: One side of the water molecule has a slightly different charge than the other side.

medium.hard: This attractive force forms specifically between a slightly positive hydrogen atom and a nearby slightly negative atom on another molecule.
medium.medium: This special attraction forms between the positive hydrogen part of one molecule and the negative part of another.
medium.easy: This is the special attraction between water molecules caused by their charged ends.

hard.hard: Breaking the extensive network of intermolecular hydrogen bonds throughout liquid water demands significantly more energy than overcoming the weaker attractions in nonpolar molecules of similar size.
hard.medium: The strong attractions between water molecules mean more heat energy is needed to separate them into gas form.
hard.easy: Water molecules stick to each other strongly, so it takes more heat to separate them into steam.

easy.text: In chemistry, what does a 'mole' represent?

options.text: A specific, very large number of particles (atoms, molecules, etc.)
options.feedback: Correct -- a mole is a counting unit, just like a 'dozen' means 12, but much larger.
That's a different meaning of the word 'mole' -- in chemistry it refers to a counting unit.
Temperature is measured in units like Celsius or Kelvin, not moles.
A mole is a counting unit for particles, not a type of bond.

medium.text: Approximately how many particles are in one mole of a substance?

options.feedback: Correct -- this is Avogadro's number, the standard count defining one mole.
This is far smaller than the actual number of particles in a mole.
This is far smaller than the actual number of particles in a mole.
12 defines a 'dozen,' not a mole -- a mole is a vastly larger quantity.

hard.text: Why is the mole such a useful unit in chemistry?

options.text: It lets chemists relate the microscopic scale of atoms/molecules to measurable, macroscopic quantities like grams
options.feedback: Correct -- the mole bridges the gap between individual particles, which are too small to count directly, and lab-scale measurements.

options.text: It makes all chemical reactions happen instantly
options.feedback: The mole is a counting unit -- it has no effect on reaction speed.

options.text: It only applies to gases, not solids or liquids
options.feedback: The mole concept applies to any substance, in any state of matter.

options.text: It replaces the need for the periodic table
options.feedback: The mole concept actually works alongside the periodic table (using atomic masses), not as a replacement for it.

easy.hard: This is a counting unit, similar in concept to how 'dozen' always means 12 of something.
easy.medium: This word describes a specific, extremely large quantity of tiny particles.
easy.easy: This is just a name for a very large counting number, like how 'dozen' means 12.

medium.hard: This number is a fixed constant used specifically to define the mole as a counting unit.
medium.medium: This is a very specific, extremely large number used to define one mole.
medium.easy: This number has 23 zeros' worth of scale -- it's Avogadro's number.

hard.hard: Atoms and molecules are far too small and numerous to count individually, so this unit connects that invisible scale to quantities you can actually weigh on a scale.
hard.medium: This unit lets scientists connect the tiny world of individual atoms to amounts they can actually measure with a scale.
hard.easy: This unit helps connect super-tiny atoms to amounts you can actually weigh and measure.

easy.text: What is required for a combustion reaction to occur?

options.feedback: Correct -- combustion reactions involve a fuel substance reacting with oxygen gas, releasing energy.
Water is not a fuel and doesn't drive combustion -- in fact, it's often used to put fires out.
Light or darkness has no role in whether combustion occurs.
Combustion typically requires heat to start, not cold temperatures.

medium.text: What are the typical products of a hydrocarbon (like methane) undergoing complete combustion?

options.feedback: Correct -- complete combustion of a hydrocarbon fuel with enough oxygen produces CO₂ and H₂O.
These are reactant-related gases, not the products formed from burning the fuel.
Salt formation isn't a product of hydrocarbon combustion.
Pure carbon (soot) can form during incomplete combustion, but complete combustion mainly produces carbon dioxide, not solid carbon.

hard.text: Why does incomplete combustion (with insufficient oxygen) produce dangerous carbon monoxide (CO) instead of carbon dioxide (CO₂)?

options.text: There isn't enough oxygen available to fully bond with every carbon atom
options.feedback: Correct -- limited oxygen means some carbon atoms only pick up one oxygen atom (forming CO) instead of two (forming CO₂).

options.text: The fuel itself contains carbon monoxide before burning starts
options.feedback: Carbon monoxide forms as a result of the incomplete reaction, not because it was already present in the fuel.

options.text: Cold temperatures during burning convert CO₂ into CO
options.feedback: This isn't related to temperature -- it's about the available oxygen supply during the reaction.

options.text: Carbon monoxide is simply a byproduct of any flame, regardless of oxygen levels
options.feedback: With sufficient oxygen, combustion mainly produces CO₂, not CO -- oxygen availability is the key factor.

easy.hard: This reaction always needs a burnable substance plus a specific gas from the air.
easy.medium: Two things are always needed: something that can burn, and a certain gas from the air.
easy.easy: Burning needs something to burn plus the gas that makes up about 21% of air.

medium.hard: Complete combustion fully oxidizes both the carbon and hydrogen atoms in the fuel into their most oxidized common forms.
medium.medium: The carbon in the fuel combines with oxygen to form one gas, and the hydrogen combines with oxygen to form a different substance.
medium.easy: One product is the same gas you exhale, and the other is the same substance as rain.

hard.hard: With oxygen scarce, each carbon atom can only bond with one oxygen atom instead of two, yielding the more dangerous, less-oxidized compound.
hard.medium: When oxygen is limited, each carbon atom only manages to grab one oxygen atom instead of the usual two.
hard.easy: Without enough oxygen around, carbon atoms only pick up one oxygen atom instead of two.

easy.text: What is the purpose of an acid-base indicator like litmus paper?

options.text: To show whether a substance is acidic or basic by changing color
options.feedback: Correct -- indicators change color depending on the pH of the substance they touch.

options.text: To measure the temperature of a substance
options.feedback: Indicators respond to acidity/basicity, not temperature.

options.text: To increase the mass of a substance
options.feedback: Indicators don't add mass -- they simply reveal a chemical property through color change.

options.text: To make a substance more reactive
options.feedback: Indicators are diagnostic tools, they don't change how reactive a substance is.

medium.text: If blue litmus paper turns red when dipped into a solution, what does this suggest about the solution?

options.feedback: Correct -- blue litmus paper turning red is the classic indicator of an acidic solution.
A basic solution would keep the litmus paper blue, or turn red litmus paper blue -- not turn blue paper red.
A neutral solution typically wouldn't cause blue litmus paper to change color at all.
Pure water is neutral and wouldn't turn blue litmus paper red.

hard.text: Phenolphthalein is colorless in acidic and neutral solutions but turns pink in basic solutions. If a chemist observes a pink color after adding phenolphthalein to an unknown solution, what can they conclude?

options.text: The solution has a pH greater than 7 (basic)
options.feedback: Correct -- phenolphthalein's pink color specifically signals a basic solution.

options.text: The solution has a pH less than 7 (acidic)
options.feedback: Phenolphthalein stays colorless in acidic solutions, so pink rules this out.

options.text: The solution is definitely pure water
options.feedback: Pure water is neutral, and phenolphthalein would remain colorless in it, not turn pink.

options.text: No conclusion can be drawn from the color
options.feedback: The color change is specifically diagnostic -- pink reliably indicates a basic solution with this indicator.

easy.hard: This tool visually reveals a chemical property through a color transformation.
easy.medium: This special paper or liquid changes color depending on acidity.
easy.easy: This special paper changes color to tell you if something is an acid or a base.

medium.hard: This particular color shift on this particular paper color is the textbook signal for one specific pH category.
medium.medium: This specific color change on blue paper is the classic sign of one particular pH category.
medium.easy: Blue paper turning red is the classic sign that something is acidic.

hard.hard: Match the observed color change to phenolphthalein's known behavior -- colorless in acid/neutral, pink specifically in basic conditions.
hard.medium: Recall that this indicator only turns pink under one specific pH condition -- basic solutions.
hard.easy: This indicator only turns pink for one type of solution -- basic ones.

easy.text: What does it mean for an element to be 'diatomic'?

options.text: It naturally exists as a molecule of two atoms bonded together
options.feedback: Correct -- diatomic elements like oxygen (O₂) are found in nature as pairs of bonded atoms.
Diatomic refers to atomic bonding structure, not color.

options.text: It can only exist as a solid
options.feedback: Diatomic elements can exist as gases, liquids, or solids -- 'diatomic' refers to bonding, not physical state.

options.text: It has two different chemical symbols
options.feedback: A diatomic element still has one chemical symbol, just written with a subscript of 2.

medium.text: Which of the following is an example of a diatomic element as it naturally occurs?

options.feedback: Correct -- nitrogen naturally exists as pairs of bonded atoms in the air.
Sodium exists as individual metal atoms in a solid lattice, not as a two-atom molecule.
Iron exists as a metallic solid made of many bonded atoms, not specifically as pairs of two.
Carbon in graphite forms extended sheets of many atoms, not simple two-atom molecules.

hard.text: Which TWO of the following elements are commonly found as diatomic molecules in their natural gaseous form?

options.feedback: Correct -- oxygen gas naturally exists as pairs of bonded oxygen atoms.
Correct -- hydrogen gas naturally exists as pairs of bonded hydrogen atoms.
Helium is a noble gas that exists as single, unbonded atoms, not in pairs.
Neon is a noble gas that exists as single, unbonded atoms, not in pairs.
Argon is a noble gas that exists as single, unbonded atoms, not in pairs.

easy.hard: This word describes a molecule built from exactly two atoms of the same element joined together.
easy.medium: This describes an element whose atoms naturally pair up, two at a time.
easy.easy: This describes an element that naturally comes in pairs of two atoms.

medium.hard: Look for an element that, in its natural gaseous state, is always found bonded in pairs rather than as standalone metal atoms or extended solid structures.
medium.medium: Look for a gas made of two identical atoms bonded together, rather than a solid metal or nonmetal structure.
medium.easy: Look for the gas that comes as pairs of two atoms bonded together, unlike the solid metals listed.

hard.hard: Two of these five are common diatomic gases; the other three are noble gases, which are famously unreactive and exist as lone, unbonded atoms.
hard.medium: Two of these are diatomic gases; the other three are noble gases that exist as single atoms, not pairs.
hard.easy: Two of these naturally pair up as two-atom molecules; the other three are noble gases that stay as single atoms.

easy.text: What is 'half-life' in the context of radioactive decay?

options.text: The time it takes for half of a radioactive sample to decay
options.feedback: Correct -- half-life measures how long it takes for half of the radioactive atoms present to decay into another form.

options.text: The total time an element can exist
options.feedback: Half-life describes a specific fraction of decay (50%), not the total existence time of an element.
Half-life is a measure of time, not a measure of an atom's mass.

options.text: The time it takes for a substance to melt
options.feedback: Melting relates to physical state changes, unrelated to radioactive decay.

medium.text: A radioactive sample has a half-life of 10 years. If you start with 100 grams, how much will remain after 20 years?

options.feedback: Correct -- after one half-life (10 years) 50g remain, and after a second half-life (20 years total) 25g remain.
This is the amount remaining after just one half-life (10 years), not two.
Half-life decay never fully reaches zero in just two half-lives -- it keeps halving the remaining amount.
This doesn't match repeatedly halving the sample over two half-life periods.

hard.text: A radioactive isotope has a half-life of 5 years. Starting with 80 grams, approximately how many years will it take to reduce to 10 grams?

options.feedback: Correct -- 80→40 (5yr)→20 (10yr)→10 (15yr), which is three half-lives.
After 10 years, only two half-lives have passed, leaving 20 grams, not 10.
This is one half-life too many -- 10 grams is reached at 15 years, not 20.
Only one half-life has passed after 5 years, leaving 40 grams, not 10.

easy.hard: This measures the duration for exactly 50% of a radioactive quantity to transform.
easy.medium: This is the amount of time it takes for exactly half of the material to break down.
easy.easy: This is how long it takes for half of a radioactive substance to decay away.

medium.hard: Divide the amount in half for each half-life period that passes -- here, that means halving it twice.
medium.medium: Cut the amount in half once for the first 10 years, then in half again for the next 10 years.
medium.easy: Cut 100 in half to get 50, then cut that in half again to get the final answer.

hard.hard: Repeatedly halve the starting amount once per half-life period elapsed, and count how many halvings are needed to reach the target amount.
hard.medium: Keep cutting the amount in half every 5 years and count how many times you need to do that to reach 10.
hard.easy: Cut 80 in half repeatedly (80→40→20→10) and count how many 5-year periods that took.
